blogs.title: Beyond Ciminelli: Why 'Pump-and-Dump' Schemes Survive the Right-to-Control Rejection
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's critical distinction between the discredited "right-to-control" theory rejected in *Ciminelli* and the viable "fraudulent-inducement" theory applied in *United States v. Constantinescu*. It examines how the court navigated the tension between protecting traditional property interests versus intangible economic information, clarifying that while depriving victims of data is not fraud, tricking them into exchanging money for securities remains a prosecutable offense even if no "informational property right" exists.

blogs.title: Intent to Defraud Without Intent to Harm: The Kousisis Standard in Social Media Fraud
blogs.description: Focusing on the mens rea requirements of securities fraud, this article explores the court's reliance on *Kousisis v. United States* to reject the defendants' argument that a lack of intent to cause net economic loss negates criminal liability. The post discusses the doctrinal shift away from requiring a "victim's bottom line" analysis, establishing that obtaining money through material misrepresentations constitutes fraud regardless of whether the victim received market-value consideration or suffered a tangible financial deficit.

blogs.title: The Digital Marketplace and Traditional Property: Redefining Fraud in the Age of Influencers
blogs.description: This piece places the *Constantinescu* decision within broader legal trends regarding white-collar crime in the digital economy. It evaluates how courts are adapting traditional mail and wire fraud doctrines—specifically borrowing from Section 1348—to address modern "pump-and-dump" schemes orchestrated via social media. The analysis considers whether this ruling expands federal jurisdiction over influencer marketing or simply reaffirms that classic deceptive practices remain illegal regardless of the platform used.
